location: Chapter 2 (The Plea and the Argument), para 0
source_text: CRITO. Yes; the meaning is only too clear. But, oh! my beloved Socrates, let me entreat you once more to take my advice and escape. For if you die I shall not only lose a friend who can never be replaced, but there is another evil: people who do not know you and me will believe that I might have saved you if I had been willing to give money, but that I did not care. Now, can there be a worse disgrace than this--that I should be thought to value money more than the life of a friend? For the many will not be persuaded that I wanted you to escape, and that you refused.
modern_text: CRITO. Yes — too clear. But Socrates, I beg you once more: take my advice and escape. If you die I lose not only an irreplaceable friend, but something else: people who don't know us will believe I could have saved you if I had been willing to spend money — and that I didn't care enough. Can there be a worse disgrace than to be thought of as someone who valued money over a friend's life? The crowd will never believe I wanted you to escape and that you refused.

location: Chapter 2 (The Plea and the Argument), para 2
source_text: CRITO. But you see, Socrates, that the opinion of the many must be regarded, for what is now happening shows that they can do the greatest evil to any one who has lost their good opinion.
modern_text: CRITO. But you can see, Socrates, that the crowd's opinion does matter. What's happening to you now shows that they can do great harm to anyone who has lost their good opinion.

location: Chapter 3 (The Laws of Athens Speak), para 2
source_text: SOCRATES. 'And was that our agreement with you?' the law would answer; 'or were you to abide by the sentence of the state?' And if I were to express my astonishment at their words, the law would probably add: 'Answer, Socrates, instead of opening your eyes--you are in the habit of asking and answering questions. Tell us,--What complaint have you to make against us which justifies you in attempting to destroy us and the state? In the first place did we not bring you into existence? Your father married your mother by our aid and begat you. Say whether you have any objection to urge against those of us who regulate marriage?' None, I should reply. 'Or against those of us who after birth regulate the nurture and education of children, in which you also were trained? Were not the laws, which have the charge of education, right in commanding your father to train you in music and gymnastic?' Right, I should reply. 'Well then, since you were brought into the world and nurtured and educated by us, can you deny in the first place that you are our child and slave, as your fathers were before you? And if this is true you are not on equal terms with us; nor can you think that you have a right to do to us what we are doing to you. Would you have any right to strike or revile or do any other evil to your father or your master, if you had one, because you have been struck or reviled by him, or received some other evil at his hands?--you would not say this? And because we think right to destroy you, do you think that you have any right to destroy us in return, and your country as far as in you lies? Will you, O professor of true virtue, pretend that you are justified in this? Has a philosopher like you failed to discover that our country is more to be valued and higher and holier far than mother or father or any ancestor, and more to be regarded in the eyes of the gods and of men of understanding? also to be soothed, and gently and reverently entreated when angry, even more than a father, and either to be persuaded, or if not persuaded, to be obeyed? And when we are punished by her, whether with imprisonment or stripes, the punishment is to be endured in silence; and if she lead us to wounds or death in battle, thither we follow as is right; neither may any one yield or retreat or leave his rank, but whether in battle or in a court of law, or in any other place, he must do what his city and his country order him; or he must change their view of what is just: and if he may do no violence to his father or mother, much less may he do violence to his country.' What answer shall we make to this, Crito? Do the laws speak truly, or do they not?
modern_text: SOCRATES. 'And was that our agreement with you?' the Laws would answer. 'Or were you to abide by the verdict of the state?' If I expressed surprise at this, the Laws would probably add: 'Answer, Socrates — instead of staring. You're used to asking and answering questions. Tell us — what complaint do you have against us that justifies you in trying to destroy us and the state? In the first place, didn't we bring you into existence? Your father married your mother through us and conceived you. Do you have any objection to those of us who govern marriage?' I would say none. 'Or against those of us who govern the upbringing and education of children, in which you yourself were trained? Were the laws governing education not right to require your father to train you in music and gymnastic?' Right, I would say. 'Well then, since you were brought into the world, raised, and educated by us — can you deny that you are our child and servant, as your forefathers were before you? And if so, you are not on equal terms with us. You cannot think you have the right to do to us what we are doing to you. Would you have any right to strike or insult or harm your father, or your master if you had one, just because you had been struck or insulted by him? — surely you would not say so. And just because we think it right to put you to death, do you think you have the right to destroy us in return — and your country, as far as you can? Will you, professor of true virtue, claim that this is justified? Has a philosopher like you failed to see that one's country is more valuable, higher and holier, than mother or father or any ancestor? More to be respected in the eyes of gods and wise men? — to be soothed and entreated when angry, even more than a father, and either to be persuaded or, if not persuaded, to be obeyed? When she punishes us — with imprisonment or beatings — the punishment must be borne in silence. If she leads us to wounds or death in battle, we follow as is right. No one may yield, retreat, or leave his post. Whether in battle, in court, or anywhere else, a man must do what his city and country command — or change their view of what is just. And if he may not do violence to his father or mother, much less may he do violence to his country.' What answer shall we give, Crito? Are the Laws speaking truly, or not?
